newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Key disputes must be settled in Cyprus, envoy says.
newsitem.headline: Key disputes must be settled in Cyprus, envoy says.

text.p: Key elements in the Cyprus dispute must be resolved if there is to be a lasting settlement on the militarily divided island, a British envoy on the conflict said on Tuesday.

British envoy Sir David Hannay, in Cyprus ahead of United Nations-sponsored talks due in New York next month between the leaders of the island's Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities, said the pending issues -- security, refugees and the geographical division of the island in a federation -- are not ones that could be worked out overnight.

"Objectively, there is a lot to be done...To sit down and write on the back of an envelope what a comprehensive settlement of Cyprus entails, it comes to quite a long list," Hannay told a news conference in Cyprus's divided capital Nicosia.

Next month Glafcos Clerides, president in the Greek Cypriot-led government, and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash will have their first face-to-face encounter in three years at the urging of the United Nations.

The international community has renewed its bid to achieve a solution to the long-standing conflict on the eastern Mediterranean island, virtually partitioned after a Turkish invasion of its north in 1974.
Last week U.S. President Bill Clinton appointed Richard Holbrooke, negotiator of the 1995 Bosnia peace accord, as special emissary for Cyprus.
The talks come against a backdrop of increased concern at the risks of militarisation of the island, and the upcoming membership talks between Cyprus and the European Union next year.

Turkish forces seized northern Cyprus in 1974 in response to a brief Greek Cypriot coup engineered by the military then ruling Greece. Some 30,000 mainland Turkish soldiers are stationed in northern Cyprus, declared a breakaway state in 1983 but recognised only by Ankara.

A solution to the Cyprus dispute has been defined as a bi-zonal, bi-communal federal state under agreements reached between the two sides in 1977 and 1979, but key differences remain on security, constitutional and territorial aspects.

"There are very difficult, very substantive differences both on the nature of the federation and on such issues as the geographical division of the two cantons, and the issue of refugees, compensation and security," said Hannay.

"These differences will have to be resolved if there is to be a settlement. That will require a lot of political will and will also require complex, technical negotiations and a lot will need to be settled in detail and in writing," he said.
